en: The Great Mārīcī Bodhisattva Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Imperial Censor of the Third Rank, Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial,
and Great Master of Illuminating Teaching, Subject Tian Xizai, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard.
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park,
together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
Together with the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
at that time the World-Honored One addressed the assembly of bhikṣus, saying:
"There is a bodhisattva named Mārīcī."
Yet that bodhisattva always travels before the sun and moon;
those suns and moons cannot see the bodhisattva,
nor can this [bodhisattva] now see them.
Neither can they be seized nor bound;
fire cannot burn them, and water cannot sweep them away.
Free from all terrors, no one dares to treat them with contempt.
None of those evil enemies shall find any opportunity against you.
O bhikṣus, in the past I knew the name of that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mārīcī;
yet they were unable to see her, unable to seize her, and unable to bind her.
Fire cannot burn it; water cannot sweep it away.
Free from all fears, no one dares to treat it with contempt.
No enemies whatsoever can invade it.
If there is a bhikṣu who knows the name of that bodhisattva,
he likewise cannot be harmed by the aforementioned evils.
Then he spoke this dhāraṇī:
*Tadyathā | oṃ bhanakrama se unayamase nīramase arikamase mṛgamase ulimase vanamase yūramase jvaramase mahājvaramase āntaridhānamase svāhā*. Furthermore, the *mārīcī-bodhisattva-dhāraṇī* is taught.
It can cause sentient beings to become invisible on roads, invisible off roads,
and invisible among the masses.
When the king of the body faces difficulties, it can conceal itself;
in all calamities such as water, fire, or bandits, it is able to remain hidden so that they find no opportunity.
Furthermore, it provides protection for those who have afflictions as well as those who are free from them.
Whether they are fainting or not fainting, all shall be protected;
even from the perils of elephant kings, lions, dragons, and tigers,
they shall provide constant protection at all times.
Then he spoke the dhāraṇī, saying:
Tadyathā | Arutārutakarū sacāru samamūridha citrakṣaṃ sarvavilambin sarvasattvaṃ śiṣya sarva...
Hambayūṃ parāve viyaḥ svāhā | Namo ratnatrayāya | Mārici-devatāye hṛdaya-māvaliteśvarī-tantraye | Tadyathā | Oṃ vandale vana-le vara-le vara-ha ||
*Mu-khye-sarba-nuṣṭha-pranuṣṭhānāṃ manda manda mukhyaṃ vaha svāhā.* Within this assembly,
there were the community of bhikṣus as well as all the bodhisattvas.
The devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and the entire great assembly,
having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and accepted it with faith.
Furthermore, the Buddha said:
If there are sentient beings who, relying upon these vast ritual procedures,
bind the seal of Mahāvairocana and visualize the radiance of the sun and moon.
In this manner, the Sun and Moon become the Bodhisattva Mārīcī;
that Bodhisattva holds a needle and thread in her hand,
sewing up the mouths and eyes of evil enemies so that they may do no harm.
The Buddha said: "That Bodhisattva Mārīcī constantly travels before the sun and moon;
although those sun and moon possess great radiance,"
Yet that Bodhisattva is not seen;
therefore, I shall now proclaim the mantra of the Great Triple Gem.

Oṃ prākrama se parākrama se unnaya se vanama se nīlama se antardhāna se svāhā. Tadyathā: āle sūkāle mūle samamūridha tsi ra kṣaṃ sarvabhaiṣajye svāhā. Oṃ vandale vanale varale varaha mukhe sarvanuṣṭhāna manda manda svāhā. If a person recites this mantra at this time:
In whatever one seeks, one must utter one's own name. Thereupon,
the Bodhisattva Mārīcī, through the power of her compassion,
acted for the sake of those sentient beings.
They provide protection on the roads;
they provide protection off the roads;
they provide protection among the crowds; and they provide protection during times of peril from water.
It shall provide protection during times of fire-related calamities, and indeed provide protection in all places whatsoever,
causing all auspicious matters to increase and flourish.
Now there is a method for accomplishment:
using fine colored silk, wooden boards, or similar materials,
one should paint an aśoka tree upon them.
Beneath this tree, one should depict the Bodhisattva Mārīcī,
her body the color of golden-yellow, appearing in the form of a young maiden,
wearing a garment of blue celestial cloth, and holding a lotus flower in her hand.
Adorned with a jeweled stūpa upon its crown;
having painted it thus, one should recite the supreme heart-mantra eight thousand times before this cloth painting.
The sought-after objective will certainly be accomplished.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ marīci svāhā. This mantra is also capable of eliminating all suffering from illness.
If a person performs homa before a painted image of the Bodhisattva Mārīcī,
they will be able to increase their elephants, horses, wealth, grain, and general prosperity;
such is the result for one who performs the homa.
If one performs one thousand *homa* offerings using curd, clarified butter, honey, and *nūriva* grass,
one will be held in high esteem by others,
remain free from illness and enjoy peace and happiness, and obtain wealth, treasures, and so forth.
If one performs a homa one thousand times using curd, rice, grains, and granulated sugar,
one can subjugate yakṣī women. If one uses mustard oil and khadira wood...
If one performs a homa of one thousand [offerings],
it can produce disease in an enemy.
If one uses one's own blood...
Performing one thousand *homa* offerings with mustard oil can slay that enemy;
if one wishes instead to pacify and eliminate the enemy's calamities, [one should perform the following].
Perform one thousand *homa* offerings using breast milk.
If you wish to eliminate all poisons and subdue the *ḍākinī* spirits,
recite the heart-mantra of Mārīcī eight hundred times every day.
Furthermore, one attains intelligence. The mantra is:

Oṃ varale vanale varāle varāhukhe sarvanuṣṭhānāṃ bandha bandha svāhā. This is the six-syllable supreme heart-mantra of the Bodhisattva Mārīcī: Oṃ mārīci svāhā. This is the mudrā for this heart-mantra.
Join the two hands in *añjali*;
let the ten fingers be slightly curved like blossoming flowers,
and then bend the two thumbs inward.
Clench the two middle fingers into the form of a fist;
sit in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka) and place the mudrā at the navel center (nābhi-cakra).
Now, this heart-seal (cittamudrā) can accomplish all matters of the supreme level.
It should be employed when seeking the most excellent and superior dharmas;
it is not permitted for use in matters of middling or inferior rank.
This heart-seal (hṛdaya-mudrā) can swiftly accomplish vast, pure, and auspicious merit;
it can swiftly eliminate all obstacles and karmic offenses,
and one shall always receive the respect of all people in every place.
The One Hundred and Eight Names Mantra of the Bodhisattva Mārīcī.
If a person constantly recites it, she will provide perpetual protection.
The mantra is as follows:

*Tadyathā:* *Arikā-mase, mṛgā-mase, unaya-mase, nīrama-se, vanama-se, yūrama-se, jvala-mase, mahājvala-mase, antardhāna-mase, svāhā.* *Namo ratnatrayāya.* *Tadyathā:* *Oṃ vandale, vanale, varale, varahe mukhe, sarvanuṣṭha-pranuṣṭhānāṃ bandha bandha muṅca svāhā.* This ritual method is extracted from the "Chapter on the Vidyādharīs."
Next, the specific method for accomplishment is explained:
the practitioner should first perform visualization,
imagining that the Bodhisattva Mārīcī is seated there.
The upper body of the golden-colored sow is clad in white garments and crowned with a jeweled stūpa;
its left hand holds a branch of an aśoka tree flower.
Furthermore, there is a herd of pigs surrounding it.
Having performed this visualization,
if one travels a long distance on the road, [one will encounter no harm].
In the event of great calamities such as bandits and the like,
take hold of the corner of one's own garment with the hand and empower that corner by reciting the heart-mantra seven times.
Furthermore, by tying the corners of that robe,
one cannot be harmed by enemies, thieves, or other such calamities.
There is yet another method for accomplishment.
First, cause the practitioner to enter samādhi.
Visualize the syllable *āṃ* upon a lunar disc.
Furthermore, contemplate that within all phenomena there is absolutely no self.
Next, visualize oneself pervading the entirety of space,
appearing in the form of Vairocana Buddha,
seated in the vajra-lotus-treasury lion throne with legs crossed in the full lotus posture.
His body is the color of pure gold, with a topknot and crown;
he forms the Vairocana mudrā and is endowed with auspicious marks and dignified majesty.
When recollecting the syllable *MĀṂ*, [he appears].
A lunar disc emits light that shines everywhere,
forming the Bodhisattva Mārīcī;
one should then recite this mantra again.
Oṃ Mārici Svāhā. At that time, the Bodhisattva held a needle and thread in her hands, and her body manifested a golden hue;
she sewed up the mouths and eyes of those evil ones so that they could no longer cause harm.
Furthermore, there is another method of accomplishment:
have a young girl prepare twenty-one strands of thread;
those that are broken should not be used.
Recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
The mantra for consecrating the thread is as follows:

*Namo ratnatrayāya, Mārīci-devatāyai, svāhā. Tadyathā: oṃ vaṃtīre vaṃtīre vaṃtare varāre varāhamukhi sarvaduṣṭapranuṣṭāna-cūrimukhaṃ bandha svāhā.* Furthermore, recite this mantra one hundred and eight times. The mantra is as follows:
*Namo māricīdevatāyai tadyathā | oṃ vandale vanale varale varahamukhe sarvanuṣṭhāgaramce mandame svāhā.* Having thus performed the recitation and empowerment, [one should proceed].
If one wishes to protect oneself,
one should tie knots with that thread;
for every seven knots, a single knot is tied.
Recite the name of Bodhisattva Mārīcī once,
and then place the cord around your neck.
Should you encounter any urgent danger while on the road, [recite it again].
Furthermore, by recollecting the mantra of the Bodhisattva Mārīcī,
both oneself and one's companions shall all attain liberation.
If one performs the ritual as previously described at one's own dwelling place, [the same result shall be achieved].
Facing the sun by day and facing the moon at the equinoxes, recite this mantra seven times.
One will certainly attain accomplishment. The mantra is as follows:
*Namo sarvabuddhabodhisattvebhyaḥ. Tadyathā: āle sūkāle mūle samamūlidhiti rakṣa rakṣa māṃ sarvabhayebhyaḥ svāhā.* The following mantras are all universally applicable:
*Oṃ varale vanale varaho mukhe sarvanuṣṭhānaṃ dhama dhama svāhā.* *Oṃ mārici svāhā.* *Oṃ varale vanale varāle vara.*
Namaḥ sarvabuddhabodhisattvebhyaḥ | Namaḥ samantānugrahapravartanāya svāhā | Oṃ marīci svāhā | Urima-maśi vanamaśi yurama-maśi jivaramaśi mahājivaramaśi antardhānamaśi | Namo.
Ratnatrayāya tadyathā oṃ vandale vanale varale varahamukhe sarvabandha bandha svāhā | Oṃ mārici svāhā | Oṃ vandale vandale vandale varale varahamukhe sarva... (Note:
The provided Sanskrit fragment appears to be a portion of a dhāraṇī mantra. The final "二" likely indicates that the text continues.)
Hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ mārici svāhā | Oṃ vandale varale varahe mukhi sarvanuṣṭha pranuṣṭhānāṃ caukimukhaṃ bandhaya svāhā | Oṃ vandale vanale ||
Varale varaha mukhe sarva nuṣṭha pranuṣṭhānām gartim bandhaya svāhā | Oṃ alika mañje svāhā | Oṃ mālīka mañje svāhā | Oṃ āndaridhana mañje svāhā ||
Namaḥ oṃ tejomaṇi svāhā | Namaḥ oṃ unnatamaṇi svāhā | Namaḥ oṃ urumāmaṇi svāhā | Namaḥ oṃ vanamaṇi svāhā | Namaḥ oṃ jvālāmaṇi svāhā | Namaḥ oṃ mahājvālāmaṇi svāhā | These and other such mantras.
It is used in the same manner as the preceding ritual procedures;
all that is sought shall be accomplished.
Furthermore, there is an accomplishment method wherein one recites this supreme heart-mantra.
Oṃ Mārici svāhā. This mantra is to be used for the rites of pacification, increase, subjugation, and magnetizing; through its application, one will certainly attain accomplishment.
Furthermore, when the practitioner performs recitation for the purpose of subjugation,
they must perform visualization,
contemplating that person as seated upon a wind-wheel.
Holding a noose and a hook with one's own hands,
one places the syllables *haḥ* and *hūṃ* within the heart of another.
Having performed the visualization,
summon those within a radius of one hundred yojanas;
whether male or female, let them all assemble.
All shall be subdued and brought into compliance, and whatever is sought shall be accomplished.
Furthermore, there is another method of accomplishment:
at the time of first emergence, one should cause a young girl to bathe and become pure.
Anointing one's body with white-flowered sandalwood and wearing white garments, one should stand at a crossroads;
this is the practice of the Kūrmācārya.
Within the maṇḍala, burn agallochum incense;
dye the thumbs of the hands with red lac and cause them to recite this mantra one hundred times.
The mantra is: Oṃ jili jili muḥ svāhā. Recite this mantra eight hundred times to consecrate the oil, and apply this oil to the top of the thumb as well.
Having applied [the ointment], the surface of the finger becomes brilliantly illuminated,
capable of manifesting the forms of devas, humans, and others.
Furthermore, recite the mantra Oṃ Āḥ eight hundred times to empower the lamp.
That maiden was able to see past events as if they were before her eyes;
she was further able to subdue all the hosts of mātṛkā spirits and could additionally recite the mantra *oṃ vandale me* many times beyond measure.
One will certainly be able to know all matters of good and evil.
Furthermore, there is an accomplishment method that can cause enemies to suffer from illness and pain, so that their attempts to harm [the practitioner] do not succeed.
Take the ashes, soil, and bone fragments of a person who has been cremated,
and further take soil from beneath the feet of one's enemy;
mix these together in one place to form a mud-paste, and fashion the shape of the enemy.
Furthermore, take poisonous substances, mustard seeds, milk, and *ariṣṭa* wood;
combine them together and write the name of the enemy,
as well as the mantra, upon the shroud of a corpse.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ mārīcy amukam jvalini gṛhṇa gṛhṇa paca hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Recite this mantra eight hundred times.
One should cause illness to arise in the enemy's house by concealing it there;
or alternatively, one may use a skull together with the aforementioned poisons, milk, and so forth.
Write the name of the enemy upon the skull,
and write the syllable *hūṃ*.
Surround the syllable *hūṃ* by writing four *ra* syllables.
Heat a human skull over a fire of khadira wood;
when that skull manifests an evil appearance,
it shall certainly cause illness by being hidden within the house of the enemy.
If one wishes to take the life of an enemy,
one should also use a mixture of poison, salt, mustard seeds, and one's own blood to create ink,
using human bone as a pen.
Furthermore, write the name of the enemy upon the skull,
as well as the two characters HŪṂ and PHAṬ;
recite the mantra eight thousand times.
He will certainly die.
The mantra is: Oṃ marici hūṃ amukamāraya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Having recited this mantra, [one should proceed].
If one buries a skull in the Śmaśāna forest,
the life-force of the enemy will perish on the third day;
this is for the purpose of causing the enemy's mind to become deranged.
Recite the mantra eight thousand times over a single crow feather;
by consecrating this feather and concealing it within the home of an enemy,
their mind will be swiftly thrown into disorder within a mere instant.
The mantra is: Oṃ mārīci cakra-pracakra-śīghra-gamini amukaṃ jambhaya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Alternatively, one may visualize the enemy riding upon a camel.
Furthermore, within a single instant, one may cause the mind to become deranged.
If one wishes to cause enemies to engage in mutual hatred,
affection, or strife, one should use the ashes of a cremated corpse, earth from both banks of a river, and earth from beneath the feet of the enemy.
Forming a mud-like mass with the same [substances], fashion the shape of an enemy;
place its face upside down.
Use the hair of water buffaloes and horses to make the cords.
To bind the body of the enemy,
use poisonous *sarṣapa* seeds mixed with oil and smear them upon that person's body;
likewise, use the blood of a water buffalo or a horse, along with the wood of the *kṣemaka* tree.
Write the name of the enemy upon a shroud from a corpse.
Write four *ṭa* syllables and write one *hūṃ* syllable in the center.
Write the character *kṣa* around its perimeter.
Place it within the heart of the enemy while reciting the mantra aloud.
Furthermore, one should visualize the enemies riding water buffaloes and horses,
attacking and killing one another;
those enemies will then harbor mutual hatred and jealousy.
The mantra is: Oṃ mārīci hūṃ amukasya vidveṣaya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Alternatively, one may use *hara* and *nuriya*. The forms of these two deities are as follows: [Description of deities].
Bury it in the Śītavana cemetery;
by reciting the aforementioned mantra, one may also cause hatred and jealousy.
Alternatively, use the horn of a water buffalo or the bone of a horse.
Form the shape of an enemy;
using poisonous medicine, mustard seeds, buffalo blood, and horse blood,
write the name of the enemy.
Upon the body of the enemy,
heat it with fire using khadira wood while reciting the aforementioned mantra once more.
In a single instant, they will come to hate and envy one another;
even the forms they have created shall be hidden within the house of their enemies.
Now I shall further explain the method for subduing enemy armies through Mahāmāricī.
If there is a kingdom whose territory is invaded by the hostile troops of a neighboring state,
and the great king of that land wishes to destroy and subdue them.
Generate profound faith and reverence for this method of accomplishment.
First, request instruction from the ācārya and make offerings according to the dharma;
then, recount the matter you seek to achieve.
At that time, the ācārya, for the sake of all sentient beings,
gave rise to a heart of compassion and entered samādhi.
Within that maṇḍala were all the articles used for offerings.
All requirements must be fully provided,
and those who participate in the ritual procedures together must not be lacking.
This is to be performed before a painted image (paṭa) of the Bodhisattva Mārīcī.
Construct a maṇḍala using white sandalwood;
offer white flowers, incense, unguents, flower garlands, and so forth,
and prepare food offerings consisting of curd, milk, and granulated sugar.
Recite the mantras for the offering of food and so forth seven times each.
The mantra is: Oṃ mārīci phat praṭiṣṭha svāhā. Recite the mantra for the fragrant unguent seven times.
Oṃ marīci gandhapradīpa svāhā. Recite this flower mantra seven times.
Oṃ marīci puṣpapradīpa svāhā. Recite this lamp mantra seven times.
Recite the incense mantra seven times: Oṃ marīci dīpa-pradīpa svāhā.
Having recited this mantra: Oṃ marīci dhūpa-pradīpa svāhā.
The ācārya generates a mind of joy and dedicates the offering to the Bodhisattva; then,
he visualizes himself in the form of Mahāvīra (the Great Hero).
Recite the mantra for subduing hostile armies three *ayuta* times. The mantra is:
Oṃ vandale vana-le vara-vāra-hum-khe sarva-ṇuṣṭhali puṣṇi-jvāla-sadhye hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Recite this mantra while maintaining pure fasting and observance of the precepts.
One will certainly see auspicious or inauspicious omens;
thereupon, one should perform the homa rite.
First, construct the homa hearth.
Use fresh, moist wood from the *pāṭala* tree, the *bodhi* tree, or the *udumbara* tree as fuel;
each piece should be twelve finger-widths long.
Dip both ends of the fuel sticks in milk, curd, and granulated sugar.
Perform eight thousand *homa* offerings using *nūriva* grass, and recite the aforementioned mantra for subduing hostile armies eight thousand times;
then all desired objectives will be accomplished. Furthermore, upon birch bark or a piece of silk—
Using kumuda incense and cow bezoar, write the mantra;
first write the name of the adversary,
and then surround it with the syllable HŪṂ.
Next, write the two characters for the name of the master of the chamber and encircle them.
Then, write the *mantra* of the Bodhisattva Maitreya in *li* script,
surrounding it on all sides so that it forms a circular pattern like a flower garland.
Furthermore, write the syllable *kṣa*, and surround it with the four syllables *aṃ*, *iṃ*, *eṃ*, and *kṣaṃ*.
Construct four gates in the four cardinal directions,
and in the four intermediate directions as well as above and below, inscribe the vajra weapons according to each respective direction.
He caused the kings, ministers,
and others to each wear one [amulet] upon their necks or upon their arms.
It can provide great protection for all military hosts;
when entering battle, weapons such as swords and blades cannot cause harm,
and one shall achieve great victory.
Furthermore, one may use the clothing of those killed by enemy soldiers, or shrouds from a charnel ground (*śmaśāna*), or the clothing of corpses.
One should also employ turmeric and yellow orpiment.
Write this mantra above it.
Furthermore, take earth from the two banks of a river and from the center of a crossroads, along with human ashes;
mix these together and fashion the form of an enemy army commander.
Using the mantra from the aforementioned scripture,
place it within the heart of the enemy commander.
Furthermore, take earth, or rice and flour, along with yellow ginger.
Combine and form them into a single pig.
Place the aforementioned enemy general within the mouth of the pig.
Furthermore, use two bowls to enclose the pig's body and carry it to the realm of the vengeful spirits,
placing it beneath the ground.
Drive a khaṇḍīva-wood stake eight finger-widths long into the center of his heart.
Offer sacrifices of pungent-flavored liquor, meat, and so forth.
Then cause the ācārya to mount an elephant or a chariot drawn by horses.
Facing the front row of the array,
place an image of the Bodhisattva Māricī upon the top of the banner;
her body is yellow in color.
The ācārya wears a golden crown upon his head and is clad in yellow robes;
holding a bell and a vajra in his hands, he generates a mind of great valor.
He further visualizes a chariot drawn by pigs as his vehicle.
Recite this mantra for subduing hostile armies eight thousand times while assuming a wrathful form;
the hostile armies will naturally be defeated, and one will swiftly achieve subjugation.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ vandale vanale varale varāhokṣe sarvārthasādhani jvālasandīpya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. This is the rite of accomplishment.
One will subdue the enemy army without further doubt.
Furthermore, there is an accomplishment method capable of subduing the enemies of others and protecting one's own assembly.
In a secluded place within the Śītavana cemetery,
one should install a painted image (paṭa) of the Bodhisattva Māricī;
before that image, one should construct a maṇḍala using cow dung.
He presents the five kinds of offerings according to his own capacity.
The ācārya himself wears black robes.
Wearing a black crown upon his head and holding a bell and a vajra in his hands,
he should generate a courageous mind and visualize the Bodhisattva Mārīcī in a wrathful form with three faces.
The face has three eyes and one is made with a boar’s face, its sharp fangs protruding outward;
the tongue is like a flash of lightning, forming a mark of great ferocity.
From the body issue flames that illuminate everywhere.
He wears garments of light equal in brilliance to twelve moons;
his body is clad in blue robes, with the right shoulder bared,
and the light is like that of a great sapphire.
His body is golden in color and adorned with various ornaments;
he has eight arms,
and in his right hands he holds a vajra and a vajra-hook.
In his left hand he holds a bow made of a branch from the *aśoka* tree and a noose;
he bears a jeweled stūpa upon his head;
he stands within a moon disc that rotates inwardly.
The right foot is in a dancing posture;
the left foot tramples upon the body of the enemy.
The ācārya recites the mantra while assuming a wrathful expression.
Furthermore, take earth from both banks of a river, human bones, powdered bone, and the ashes of cremated corpses;
mix these together to fashion the form of an enemy.
Then, employ pungent and bitter substances, poisonous drugs, salt, mustard seeds, and the juice of the *mandāra* flower.
Place it upon the shroud of the corpse;
write the name of the enemy and the mantra thereon,
and cause them likewise to enter into the heart of the enemy.
The mantra is:
Oṃ vandale vanale varale varāhākṣi hūṃ amukasya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Furthermore, use the flesh of a dried corpse and guggulu incense.
Form it into a pill together with the practitioner.
Moisten the medicine with human fat,
and use fire from the charred wood of a cremated corpse along with mustard oil.
Perform eight thousand homas;
during each homa, recite the name of the King of the Army of Vengeful Spirits.
Once this rite has been completed:
If one wishes to bind them, they are immediately bound;
if one wishes to kill them, they may be killed.
Or, the ācārya may face the enemy host.
Performing *homa* with powdered human bone and human fat mixed with mustard oil,
one’s enemy army will descend [in submission] in a single instant while reciting the mantra.
Furthermore, there is another method of accomplishment.
It can pacify calamities affecting domestic animals.
If one wishes to perform the rite,
use white sandalwood, *guggulu*, and ox-gall together, blending them into a paste.
Write the mantra upon a white banner and place it within the gatehouse of the livestock stable; furthermore, write the mantra on paper and have those who tend the cattle carry it upon their heads.
Furthermore, place another copy upon the head of the animal;
therein, write these four characters of the mantra: *Aṃ Āṃ Eṃ Āṃ*.
Next, surround them by writing the character *Bha*.
Furthermore, write the syllable *kṣa* once around [the perimeter].
Having written it in this manner,
take khadira wood to fashion a stake eight finger-widths long.

Like a supreme lotus jewel,

When there is a drought, administer seven pills into the dragon pond,

securing it with a blue thread.

Then, construct a maṇḍala.

With a branch of pomegranate, wipe the dragon’s body twenty-one times.

That nāga, finding no pleasure in its own palace, comes to be subdued.

Again, perform the visualization:
imagine arrows like clusters of *nyagrodha* flowers shooting into his heart.

if one performs the rite of subjugation, [the same applies].
The ritual procedures are as before.

Having visualized that one is subduing those persons by pulling them with nooses and hooks, one should then recite the mantra;

one should mix poison, mustard seeds, and the juice of *ariṣṭa* wood together;

then, bind that form tightly with the hair of a water buffalo and a horse.

Having formed this visualization,
one should roast that image over a fire of khadira wood while reciting the mantra an incalculable number of times.
Because that form is hidden beneath the house or in the Śītavana cemetery,

Furthermore, regarding the method for binding and restraining the wicked:
take poisonous drugs, mustard seeds, realgar, yellow ginger juice, and red earth, and blend them together.
Write the mantra-wheel for binding upon birch bark;
place the wheel inside a single bowl and cover it completely with ashes.
Furthermore, cover it with a bowl and hide it in a secret place.
Recite the mantra many times, numbering in the hundreds of millions (ayuta).
That person will immediately be bound and restrained.
Furthermore, regarding the rite for dispatching adversaries:
use red-colored poison and the juice of the *ṭakṣecchima* wood to mix together as ink.
Using a crow’s wing as a brush,
one should write the *visarjana-mantra* (the mantra for dismissal) on a cloth from a corpse or upon leaves of the *pārśa* tree and so forth, forming the shape of Cintāmaṇicakra.
Then, having recited the mantra many times— countless as the sands of the Ganges—
he fastened the wheel around the crow's neck and released it toward the northwest.
Alternatively, it may also be done in the south.
Within a mere moment, the enemy will naturally retreat.
Furthermore, here is the rite for destroying enemies.
Mix poison, salt, mustard seeds, and blood from one's own finger in a single place; using a human bone as a pen,
inscribe the mantra wheel upon a corpse’s garment or on a skull.
Furthermore, take human ashes, powdered bones, pure earth, soil from under the feet of an enemy, and poisons;
mix these together to form a clay image of the enemy.
Place the mantra-wheel within the heart of that image.
At midday, one should roast the image over a fire of khadira wood while facing south and visualizing it.
Upon the index finger, there are three black pig heads.
Recite the mantra many times, beyond measure.
Furthermore, visualize the form of the enemy before you, shattered into countless fragments.
Having visualized that hundreds of thousands of vultures, crows, and ravens are devouring those enemies,
one should imagine them hidden beneath the enemy's house or in a charnel ground filled with corpses.
Within three days, the life of the enemy shall end.
Next, regarding the method for requesting rain:
according to the ritual procedures as before, one should first visualize Vairocana Buddha.
Next, visualize all the worthy sages upon the wish-fulfilling jewel wheel,
holding vessels of nectar as if executing the Master’s command;
recite the mantra for the dragon throughout the day.
Immediately upon entering samādhi, the dragon will send down rain.
Furthermore, regarding the method for seeking rain:
use *kunkuma* incense, white sandalwood, and blue pigment (*añjana*).
Write the mantra wheel upon birch bark.
Then, take earth from a beaten clay pot and fashion it into the form of a nāga.
Tie the mantra wheel with a blue thread around the neck of the nāga.
Place one bowl of breast milk inside the nāga and cover it with another bowl;
seal it with the Vajra-mudrā.
He continued to recite the mantra for many incalculable times (*asaṃkhyeya*).
He then sent the nāga into the nāga-shrine, whereupon a great rain fell.
Furthermore, this is the method for seeking rain.
Using poisons and the like,
one should inscribe the mantra-cakra upon a cloth from a corpse or upon a broken earthenware jar.
At the hub of the wheel, write the two characters "Ṭa" and "Ṭha.
On the eastern spoke of the wheel, depict the great nāga king Ananta;
on the southern spoke, depict the nāga king Vāsuki.
On the western spoke, the nāga king Takṣaka is depicted;
on the northern spoke, the nāga king Karkoṭaka is depicted;
and on the southeastern spoke, the nāga king Śaṅkhapāla is depicted.
On the spoke in the southwest, paint the Great Lotus Nāga King; on the spoke in the northwest, paint the Lotus Nāga King;
and on the spoke in the northeast, paint the Kulika Nāga King.
On the rim of the wheel, draw all the rain-bringing nāgas and write the rain-bringing mantra;
furthermore, perform the visualization in this manner.
Visualize the Bodhisattva Māricī in the midst of the fire of khadira wood,
manifesting a wrathful form.
Having visualized her, recite the mantra many times, numbering in the hundreds of thousands (ayuta).
A great rain will fall quickly.
If the rain does not cease,
take gold dust, realgar, and yellow ginger, and mix them together.
Write the mantra upon a clay bowl,
cover the bowl completely with ash,
and tie it with yellow thread.
One should make an offering of yellow flowers and recite the mantra many times, numbering in the hundreds of thousands (ayuta);
the rain will then quickly cease.
Furthermore, regarding the rite for subduing enemies:
take poisons and other substances and write the mantra of Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, as well as the root mantra, upon a cloth from a corpse.
Concealing it in a secret place,
one should recite the mantra many times, numbering in the tens of millions,
while walking about as one pleases.
All enemies will naturally be restrained.
Furthermore, regarding the method for restraining hostile armies so that they do not invade the borders:
if the king places deep faith in the Buddha-dharma and reveres the ācārya, [the enemy forces will be halted].
When performing this rite of the maṇḍala, one must certainly not trespass;
use realgar and ginger juice upon a shroud from a corpse.
Write down the mantra of the Bodhisattva Maśī and the name of the adversary;
this serves as a wish-fulfilling jewel-wheel (*cintāmaṇicakra*).
Take earth from both banks of a river, earth from the center of a crossroads, or earth from a mountain, along with the ashes of a burnt human.
Fashion a clay image of the enemy’s general,
and place the mantra-wheel within its heart.
Then, fashion another clay image of a pig.
The mouth of a pig contains the feet of a soldier of resentment;
its body hangs halfway down,
all resting within a single bowl.
Then, using another bowl, join them together.
Take them to a place within the territory of the enemy forces and bury them there; drive a khadira-wood stake eight finger-widths long into the top of the effigy of the enemy.
One should perform the birth-rite sacrifice using food, drink, wine, and meat.
At that time, the ācārya should suspend a painted image of Mārīcī;
on the back of the cloth, he should inscribe the mantra as desired.
Place it upon the banner and pennants.
Assume a wrathful form like that of Vajrasattva,
and then recite the mantra many times, numbering in the hundreds of millions (ayuta).
Riding an elephant chariot, he went before that army;
his enemies bound his hands and feet with ropes,
so that he could display no valor and withdrew in fear.
Furthermore, regarding the rite for pacifying calamities (*śāntika*):
first, generate food according to one's inclination and offer it as a universal offering.
Then, perform mental visualization within one's own mind.
Visualize that all the worthy sages and holy ones of the wish-fulfilling jewel wheel protect the people of the world.
Having thus invoked them according to the ritual,
make offerings with amṛta water.
Then recite this mantra:
Oṃ kha kha khāhi khāhi gṛhṇa gṛhṇa sarvabhūtān kāvye mama śāntiṃ kuru svāhā. Having recited this mantra, [proceed].
Both oneself and others shall attain the pacification of calamities.
Furthermore, regarding the method for praying for clear weather when rain persists for a long time:
have the reciter perform the following visualization.
Visualize the Bodhisattva Mārīcī as the color of black smoke,
with a large belly, a fierce and wrathful countenance, and a wrathful gaze.
Furthermore, visualize the mantra-wheel upon the Bodhisattva.
In the space between [the teeth],
it is like trees withered by the fire at the end of a great kalpa.
Having formed this perception, one immediately extends the tongue to lick and eat [them].
In the blink of an eye, the sky became clear and bright.
Furthermore, as for the rite of binding by prohibition:
use realgar, the juice of yellow ginger, and red earth.
Gather them together in one place.
Within a copper vessel, draw the figure of that person,
and further, upon the heart, inscribe the wheel of the mantra for binding and subduing.
Place it in water at a secluded location and perform offerings with yellow flowers while reciting the mantra;
all enemies and malicious persons who come or go will be bound and restrained.
Furthermore, regarding the method for causing the minds of enemies to become deluded and confused:
as previously described in the *Amoghapāśa* [Sūtra],
one should write down the mantra for delusion and so forth.
Mix soil from a place where a person urinates with the juice of *mantāra* wood to fashion the form of the enemy.
Place the mantra-wheel within the heart of that form.
Having roasted that form over a fire in the Śmaśāna forest,
one should recite the mantra many times, numbering in the hundreds of millions (ayuta),
and then immediately bury that form beneath the house of the enemy.
One will quickly fall into confusion.
Alternatively, one may place the seeds of the *mantara* plant inside meat and submerge it in water for seven days.
Take it out and give it to the enemy to eat;
whether mixed with wine or used as incense, it will cause them to become deluded and confused.
If one wishes to remove this delusion and confusion, [one must perform the following].
Bathe one's own body with breast milk and recite the mantra many times, beyond counting;
one will immediately attain the pacification of calamities and be restored to one's former state.
Furthermore, if there is a woman who is deeply attached to her husband and one wishes to cause him to despise and abandon her,
one should use the juice of the *kṣemaka* flower.
In the absence of this flower juice, one should use poison and blood from one's own fingertip,
mixing them together; then,
as before, write the mantra and the husband's name upon a shroud from a corpse.
Dip the wheel with lacquer resin,
then heat it over a fire of jujube wood while reciting the mantra many times, numbering in the tens of millions (ayuta).
By burying the wheel of mantras beneath the threshold,
the husband will immediately give rise to aversion and cease his attachment.
Furthermore, if a woman wishes for others to love and respect her, [she should do so].
Using cow bezoar, the juice of *śrīvṛkṣa* leaves, and human blood,
one should inscribe the mantra-cakra together with one's own name upon birch bark.
Then, recite the mantra many times, numbering in the hundreds of millions (*ayuta*).
By consecrating that wheel and wearing it upon one's neck,
one will immediately be revered and loved by others.
Such is the mantra of the Bodhisattva Mārīcī and others.
If an ācārya maintains this according to the ritual rules and constantly recites it,
there is no sought-after objective that will not be accomplished—
namely, the sacred sword, eye-salve, sandals, and medicinal pills.
She subdues yakṣīs, devīs, nāgīs, asurīs, kinnarīs,
and so forth, causing them all to become compliant,
respectful, affectionate, and harmonious.
By the power of the mantra and the majestic authority of that vidyādhara—
just like the supernatural might of the Bodhisattva Mārīcī—
all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas [are subdued].
Kakuda-bhujangas, piśācas, rākṣasas, mātṛs, kinnaras, uṣadarakas, preta-bodies, and bhūtas.
Even the great luminaries of the deluding spirits, Vaitāḍhya-jīvakas,
and their retinues of various malevolent ghosts who harbor evil intentions cannot even invade the shadow of that vidyādhara.
How much more so, then, to harm their very bodies?
Therefore, the Vidyādhara Ācārya is able to attain pure and great merit.
It can increase and expand great auspiciousness,
eliminate all grave sins,
and accomplish the samādhi of the deity.
When you realize the Dharmakāya of Vairocana,
you all should faithfully accept, read, and recite this Mārīcī Sūtra.
Furthermore, there are methods for pacifying calamities, increasing prosperity, and so forth.
At the time of commencement, there are specific periods for each:
the rite for pacifying calamities is performed in the early morning,
and the rite for increasing prosperity is likewise performed in the early morning.
The rite for subjugation is performed at midday;
the rite for endearment is performed at midnight.
Thus, the physical characteristics of these four rites each differ.
For the rite of pacification (śāntika), the implements used and the clothing of the vidyādhara shall both be white.
For the rite of augmentation (pauṣṭika), the implements used and the clothing of the ācārya shall both be yellow.
For the rite of attraction (vaśīkaraṇa), the implements used and the robes of the ācārya shall both be red.
For the rite of subjugation (abhicāra), the implements used and the robes of the ācārya shall both be black.
As previously described, there are twenty-two types of ritual applications for writing mantras upon the wish-fulfilling jewel wheel (*cintāmaṇicakra*).
By seeking all matters through these, they shall all be truly realized and none fail to be accomplished.
That Ācārya, by means of this ritual procedure, attains mastery over the secret.
This King of Mantras is supreme and foremost.
With a focused mind, take refuge and pay homage to the Bodhisattva Mārīcī.
The methods for accomplishment taught by the Buddha Vairocana—
relying upon this supreme ritual manual, may the Compassionate One speak them once more.
If we are able to hear them, we shall forever be freed from all perils and hardships.
Furthermore, if there is a disciple who has received empowerment within a maṇḍala and,
following the instructions of their own master, maintains their fundamental samaya;
Having generated a pure mind and sought the unsurpassed path to deliver all sentient beings,
one should first recite this mantra before performing these rites.
Having recited the mantra *Oṃ hūṃ phaṭ*,
form the wrathful fist with the hand and place it upon the heart,
the neck, the forehead, and the crown of the head.
Immediately rinse the mouth with water and enter the Hall of the Noble Ones to gaze upon the paṭa of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī.
Recite the mantra for expelling māras to consecrate the perfumed water.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ marīci hūṃ sarvavijñānanuśodhana svāhā. Having recited this mantra, one should immediately perform the visualization.
Visualize that within one's own heart, the syllable *āḥ* transforms into a moon disc,
and the syllable *aṃ* transforms into a sun disc;
the appearance of these sun and moon is like the color of molten gold.
Again, there emerges the light of the *karmavācanā*, which transforms into a Perfectly Enlightened One, a Teacher of Gods and Humans;
one then personally pays homage, presents various offerings, and recites the mantra.
Oṃ marīci bhaṅktaṃ pratīccha svāhā. Recite this mantra to offer food and drink to the Buddha.
Oṃ marīci puṣpa-pratīccha svāhā. Reciting this mantra, offer flowers to the Buddha.
Oṃ marīci-dūpaṃ pratyakṣa svāhā. Recite this mantra to offer incense to the Buddha.
Oṃ marīci ne pañca-pratīccha svāhā. Recite this mantra to offer a lamp to the Buddha.
Oṃ marīci-gandha-pratīccha svāhā. Recite this mantra to offer scented unguent to the Buddha.
Recite this mantra: Oṃ marīci svāhā. Consecrate the argha water with this mantra and present each offering in this manner one by one.
If one lacks the power to provide such offerings as food and drink,
one should instead perform each offering through visualization.
In this way, one takes refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha— the truly pure field of merit.
Having repented and confessed all karmic obstructions and transgressions, one makes the following vow for the dedication of all roots of goodness arising from sympathetic joy:
"I have awakened the bodhicitta; Whatever merits I have performed..."
Dedicating this toward True Suchness, pervading the entire Dharma-realm and all sentient beings,
may they all equally partake in benefit and bliss,
universally resolve upon the Unsurpassed Mind, and together attain Perfect Enlightenment.
Having thus recited the verse three times,
he immediately entered samādhi and contemplated that all dharmas are devoid of self.
Having performed this visualization, one should recite the mantra of selflessness:
*Oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako haṃ*. Having recited the mantra, one enters samādhi once again.
Contemplate that subtle characters are like illusions and transformations, lacking any real nature.
Next, contemplate the three realms, the six destinies, the four modes of birth, and the nine abodes;
as well as the five objects of the senses, such as form, and the internal and external four great elements.
Arising solely from conditions, they possess no substantial reality at all;
because all natures are empty and not separate from consciousness,
once one has contemplated in this way, all karmic obstructions of the past and present are entirely eliminated.
Then, recite the mantra for the purification of the three karmas:
Oṃ svabhāva-śuddhāḥ sarva-dharmāḥ svabhāva-śuddho ’haṃ. Recite this mantra three times.
He immediately enters samādhi.
He further visualizes the syllable Oṃ upon the wish-fulfilling jewel wheel,
which transforms into Vairocana Buddha.
Upon a lion throne within the Lotus Treasury,
he sits in the vajra-paryaṅka posture;
his body is golden in color, and he forms the Vairocana mudrā as a sign of entering meditative absorption.
He possesses a topknot and crown, complete with all ornaments.
Upon the heart of that Buddha is a moon disc,
upon which are the fifth and sixth subtle Brahma-syllables.
Possessing the essence of the first and second tones like the Dharma-realm,
and further, upon those subtle syllables,
there are the sun and moon, with a color like that of *candana* gold.
All Tathāgatas uphold this syllable;
it can further be transformed into a five-pronged vajra,

That vajra, by means of its supernormal power,

beneath the pavilion are eight pillars,

In the center of the maṇḍala, place eight heavy vajras.

furthermore, it was encircled on all sides by vajras,

Oṃ ālika-maṣe svāhā. Install this bodhisattva in the eastern direction.
Her body is red in color, with the appearance of a young maiden.

Oṃ mārici maṣe svāhā. Install this bodhisattva in the southern direction.
Her body is golden in color, like that of a young maiden;
she wears garments of blue celestial silk and is adorned with every ornament.

Oṃ āḥ dīrgha-mukhe svāhā. One should place this Bodhisattva in the north.
Their bodies have the color of the rising sun and the appearance of young maidens, clad in garments as blue as the sky and adorned with every ornament;
